topic: 7 borders that make no sense, ending on India's Tin Bigha Corridor
hook: Your drive across Brunei used to cross Malaysia twice, with passport stamps both ways, just to stay inside one country.
title: 7 Borders That Make No Sense, Ending in India
description:
Seven real borders that look fake on the map: Brunei, The Gambia, Nakhchivan, Cabinda, Oecusse, Dahagram-Angarpota and India's Tin Bigha Corridor. Each one is shown on a simple map with the odd shape highlighted. The last one is a strip of Indian land leased to Bangladesh.

#borders #geography #india
comment_prompt: Which border would you want to cross first?

scenes.narration: Your drive across Brunei used to cross Malaysia twice, with passport stamps both ways, just to stay inside one country.
scenes.headline: One Country, Two Stamps

scenes.narration: That is not even the strangest border in this video, and by the end you'll see why.
scenes.headline: Stranger Is Coming

scenes.narration: Today we count down seven real borders that make no sense, and each one is stranger than the one before.
scenes.headline: 7 Strange Borders

scenes.narration: The last one is in India: a strip of Indian land, leased to another country, with a gate in the middle.
scenes.headline: India's Strangest

scenes.narration: Every place here is real and on the map today. We start at number seven and end in India.
scenes.headline: All Real

scenes.narration: Number seven: Brunei, a small country on the island of Borneo that comes in two separate pieces.
scenes.headline: 7: Brunei

scenes.narration: On the map, Brunei looks like a shape with a bite taken out of it, and the bite is not part of Brunei.
scenes.headline: A Bite Out Of Brunei

scenes.narration: That bite is Limbang, a district of the Malaysian state of Sarawak, and it splits Brunei's eastern part from the rest.
scenes.headline: Limbang Splits It

scenes.narration: The eastern piece is called Temburong. To drive from Temburong to the capital side, you left Brunei, entered Malaysia, then came back.
scenes.headline: Leave, Enter, Return

scenes.narration: That meant border checks and passport stamps in both directions, all for one trip inside a single country.
scenes.headline: Passport Stamps

scenes.narration: Limbang became part of Sarawak in 1890, when the White Rajah of Sarawak took it over, and it never went back.
scenes.headline: Taken In 1890

scenes.narration: In 2009, Brunei and Malaysia signed a deal, and Brunei gave up its claim to Limbang for good.
scenes.headline: 2009 Deal

scenes.narration: In 2020, Brunei opened a long bridge across its bay, so drivers can now skip Malaysia, but the odd shape remains.
scenes.headline: New Bridge, Same Map

scenes.narration: A country in two pieces is strange. But the next one is a whole country that is basically a river.
scenes.headline: Next: A River Country

scenes.narration: Number six: The Gambia, the country in West Africa that looks like a long thin snake lying across the map.
scenes.headline: 6: The Gambia

scenes.narration: It follows the Gambia River inland, and it is only a thin strip, roughly twenty-five to fifty kilometres wide.
scenes.headline: A Thin Strip

scenes.narration: Senegal surrounds it on every side except the short Atlantic coast, so nearly every border you cross there leads into Senegal.
scenes.headline: Wrapped By Senegal

scenes.narration: The shape comes from colonial days, when Britain controlled the river and France controlled the land all around it.
scenes.headline: Colonial Leftovers

scenes.narration: The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa, and its capital, Banjul, sits right where the river meets the Atlantic.
scenes.headline: Banjul At The Mouth

scenes.narration: In 1982, Gambia and Senegal even tried joining together as one country called Senegambia, but it fell apart in 1989.
scenes.headline: Senegambia Failed

scenes.narration: A country shaped like a river is odd. Now imagine a piece of your country that you cannot reach by land.
scenes.headline: Next: Cut Off

scenes.narration: Number five: Nakhchivan, a part of Azerbaijan that has no land connection to the rest of Azerbaijan.
scenes.headline: 5: Nakhchivan

scenes.narration: It sits to the west, cut off from the main country by a strip of Armenia in between.
scenes.headline: Armenia In The Way

scenes.narration: Its land borders are with Armenia, Iran and Turkey. The one country it cannot touch by land is its own mainland.
scenes.headline: Three Neighbours

scenes.narration: Azerbaijan runs it as an autonomous republic with its own parliament, which makes it a whole region sitting alone.
scenes.headline: A Region Alone

scenes.narration: Most people have reached it by plane, because the land route through Armenia was closed for decades.
scenes.headline: Fly Instead

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places like these, subscribe, because we find a new one every day.
scenes.headline: More Strange Places

scenes.narration: Stay with me. The next one is an oil-rich region sitting on the wrong side of another country.
scenes.headline: Next: Oil And A Gap

scenes.narration: Number four: Cabinda, a piece of Angola that sits on the other side of a different country.
scenes.headline: 4: Cabinda

scenes.narration: Angola is in southern Africa, but Cabinda is up north, split away by a slice of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
scenes.headline: Split By DR Congo

scenes.narration: That slice is the DR Congo's only access to the Atlantic, where the huge Congo River reaches the sea.
scenes.headline: Congo's Door To Sea

scenes.narration: So the DR Congo gets a narrow door to the ocean, and that same door cuts Angola into two pieces.
scenes.headline: One Door, Two Angolas

scenes.narration: Cabinda has also been a major source of Angola's oil, which is why this odd shape matters so much.
scenes.headline: Oil Matters

scenes.narration: It became a Portuguese protectorate under a treaty in 1885, and it was handled separately from the rest of Angola.
scenes.headline: Treaty Of 1885

scenes.narration: A group called FLEC has argued for decades that Cabinda should be its own country.
scenes.headline: Own Country Demand

scenes.narration: Most travellers fly between the two, because going by road means crossing into DR Congo and back out.
scenes.headline: Fly, Don't Drive

scenes.narration: Cut-off pieces are strange. But the next piece sits on an island that belongs mostly to someone else.
scenes.headline: Next: Island Piece

scenes.narration: Number three: Oecusse, a piece of East Timor that sits on the island of Timor, inside Indonesian land.
scenes.headline: 3: Oecusse

scenes.narration: East Timor's main part is far to the east, but Oecusse sits on the north coast of the western half.
scenes.headline: Far From Home

scenes.narration: Indonesian West Timor wraps around it on the land sides, so there is no land link to the rest of East Timor.
scenes.headline: Wrapped By Indonesia

scenes.narration: To drive from Dili to Oecusse, you leave East Timor, cross a stretch of Indonesia, then enter East Timor again.
scenes.headline: Out And Back In

scenes.narration: There is also a ferry along the coast, so travellers can stay in East Timor's waters the whole way.
scenes.headline: The Sea Route

scenes.narration: The Portuguese built an early capital at Lifau, in Oecusse, so this land has a longer history than the country itself.
scenes.headline: Older Than The Country

scenes.narration: East Timor became independent in 2002, and Oecusse stayed part of it, even though Indonesia surrounds it on land.
scenes.headline: Independent 2002

scenes.narration: Now we're coming home, because the last two borders are both in India's state of West Bengal.
scenes.headline: Now, India

scenes.narration: And number two is a village where the land around you is India, but the village itself is not.
scenes.headline: A Village Not In India

scenes.narration: Number two: Dahagram and Angarpota, two Bangladeshi villages that sit inside the Indian state of West Bengal.
scenes.headline: 2: Dahagram

scenes.narration: In 2015, India and Bangladesh swapped 162 small enclaves, so that people could finally belong to the country around them.
scenes.headline: The 2015 Swap

scenes.narration: Dahagram and Angarpota were not part of that swap. They stayed Bangladeshi, linked to Bangladesh by one special strip.
scenes.headline: Left Out Of The Swap

scenes.narration: Under the old treaty the area is about eighteen square kilometres, and by some estimates around twenty thousand people live there.
scenes.headline: Around 20,000 People

scenes.narration: On almost every side there is only Indian land. Walk out of almost any side and you step onto Indian soil.
scenes.headline: India On Every Side

scenes.narration: For decades, reaching the rest of Bangladesh meant crossing Indian land, with no agreed right to do so.
scenes.headline: No Agreed Road

scenes.narration: The fix was a deal, and the deal is a tiny strip of India. That strip is number one.
scenes.headline: The Deal

scenes.narration: Number one: the Tin Bigha Corridor, the strangest border in India, and it is smaller than you'd think.
scenes.headline: 1: Tin Bigha

scenes.narration: The treaty puts it at about 178 metres by 85 metres, a distance you could walk in a few minutes.
scenes.headline: Tiny Strip

scenes.narration: India leased this strip to Bangladesh, so Bangladeshi citizens can pass through it to reach Dahagram and Angarpota.
scenes.headline: Leased To Bangladesh

scenes.narration: Think about that. The ground is Indian, but the people crossing it are Bangladeshi, heading to Bangladeshi villages.
scenes.headline: Indian Soil, Foreign Walkers

scenes.narration: Its name uses bigha, an old land measure used across India, and tin simply means three.
scenes.headline: Tin Means Three

scenes.narration: A gate controls the corridor, and guards check everyone who goes through, as they would at any border.
scenes.headline: The Gate

scenes.narration: In the early years, that gate opened for only a short time each day, so villagers lived by the clock.
scenes.headline: Open Only Some Hours

scenes.narration: Imagine running to beat a gate that closes, just to reach your own village in your own country.
scenes.headline: Beat The Gate

scenes.narration: Today the corridor stays open day and night, but people still need permission to cross it.
scenes.headline: Open Day And Night

scenes.narration: For the people of Dahagram, this strip is the road to the rest of their own country.
scenes.headline: Their Only Road

scenes.narration: India still owns the strip, and Bangladesh has the right to use it. That is a very unusual arrangement anywhere in the world.
scenes.headline: Owned By One, Used By Other

scenes.narration: One small rectangle of land shows how far a border can bend to fit the lives of real people.
scenes.headline: Borders Can Bend

scenes.narration: So that was the full countdown: Brunei, The Gambia, Nakhchivan, Cabinda, Oecusse, Dahagram and Angarpota, and the Tin Bigha Corridor.
scenes.headline: The Full Countdown

scenes.narration: Each one is real and on your map. Most began when someone drew a line without thinking of the people living there.
scenes.headline: Lines Drawn Far Away

scenes.narration: Which brings us back to the start: your drive across Brunei really did cross Malaysia twice, with passport stamps both ways.
scenes.headline: Back To Brunei

scenes.narration: And the strangest border of all is not far away. It is a gate on Indian soil, built for another country's villagers.
scenes.headline: India Wins Weirdest

scenes.narration: Next video: the Indian neighbour whose clocks run fifteen minutes ahead of ours.
scenes.headline: Next: Nepal's Clock
